entries.b70831816b68efd1257cda0ea148fb75c56d2053: <div eID="gen13636" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Weighty Sayings.</title> <div sID="gen13637" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> A false balance <hi type="italic">is</hi> abomination to the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : but a just weight <hi type="italic">is</hi> his delight. <div eID="gen13637" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13638" type="x-p"/> As religion towards God is a branch of universal righteousness (he is not an honest man that is not devout), so righteousness towards men is a branch of true religion, for he is not a godly man that is not honest, nor can he expect that his devotion should be accepted; for, 1. Nothing is more offensive to God than deceit in commerce. <hi type="italic">A false balance</hi> is here put for all manner of unjust and fraudulent practices in dealing with any person, which are all an <hi type="italic">abomination to the Lord,</hi> and render those abominable to him that allow themselves in the use of such accursed arts of thriving. It is an affront to justice, which God is the patron of, as well as a wrong to our neighbour, whom God is the protector of. Men make light of such frauds, and think there is no sin in that which there is money to be got by, and, while it passes undiscovered, they cannot blame themselves for it; a blot is no blot till it is hit, <reference osisRef="Hos.12.7-Hos.12.8">Hos. xii. 7, 8</reference>. But they are not the less an abomination to God, who will be the avenger of those that are defrauded by their brethren. 2. Nothing is more pleasing to God than fair and honest dealing, nor more necessary to make us and our devotions acceptable to him: <hi type="italic">A just weight is his delight.</hi> He himself goes by a just weight, and holds the scale of judgment with an even hand, and therefore is pleased with those that are herein followers of him. A balance cheats, under pretence of doing right most exactly, and therefore is the greater abomination to God.
entries.f45cd37eb14fa71aeb76f19c2a740da48b34c4cc: <div eID="gen13638" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13639" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">2</hi> <hi type="italic">When</hi> pride cometh, then cometh shame: but with the lowly <hi type="italic">is</hi> wisdom. <div eID="gen13639" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13640" type="x-p"/> Observe, 1. How he that exalts himself is here abased, and contempt put upon him. <hi type="italic">When pride comes then comes shame.</hi> Pride is a sin which men have reason to be themselves ashamed of; it is a shame to a man who springs out of the earth, who lives upon alms, depends upon God, and has forfeited all he has, to be proud. It is a sin which others cry out shame on and look upon with disdain; he that is haughty makes himself contemptible; it is a sin for which God often brings men down, as he did Nebuchadnezzar and Herod, whose ignominy immediately attended their vain-glory; for God <hi type="italic">resists the proud,</hi> contradicts them, and counterworks them, in the thing they are proud of, <reference osisRef="Isa.2.11">Isa. ii. 11</reference>, &c. 2. How he that humbles himself is here exalted, and a high character is given him. As with the proud there is folly, and will be shame, so <hi type="italic">with the lowly there is wisdom,</hi> and will be honour, for a man's wisdom gains him respect and makes his face to shine before men; or, if any be so base as to trample upon the humble, God will give them grace which will be their glory. Considering how safe, and quiet, and easy, those are that are of a humble spirit, what communion they have with God and comfort in themselves, we will say, <hi type="italic">With the lowly is wisdom.</hi>
entries.5070d105edba716a7ed052027fc4f01d11971583: <div eID="gen13640" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Advantages of the Righteous.</title> <div sID="gen13641" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">3</hi> The integrity of the upright shall guide them: but the perverseness of transgressors shall destroy them. <div eID="gen13641" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13642" type="x-p"/> It is not only promised that God will guide the upright, and threatened that he will destroy the transgressors, but, that we may be the more fully assured of both, it is here represented as if the nature of the thing were such on both sides that it would do it itself. 1. The integrity of an honest man will itself be his guide in the way of duty and the way of safety. His principles are fixed, his rule is certain, and therefore his way is plain; his sincerity keeps him steady, and he needs not tack about every time the wind turns, having no other end to drive at than to keep a good conscience. <hi type="italic">Integrity and uprightness</hi> will <hi type="italic">preserve</hi> men, <reference osisRef="Ps.25.21">Ps. xxv. 21</reference>. 2. The iniquity of a bad man will itself be his ruin. As the plainness of a good man will be his protection, though he is ever so much exposed, so the perverseness of sinners will be their destruction, though they think themselves ever so well fortified. They shall fall into pits of their own digging, <reference osisRef="Prov.5.22">ch. v. 22</reference>.
entries.5676daea95ad233983a2daddf761c4fb001df180: <div eID="gen13642" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13643" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">4</hi> Riches profit not in the day of wrath: but righteousness delivereth from death. <div eID="gen13643" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13644" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. The <hi type="italic">day of death</hi> will be a <hi type="italic">day of wrath.</hi> It is a messenger of God's wrath; therefore when Moses had meditated on man's mortality he takes occasion thence to admire <hi type="italic">the power of God's anger,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.110.11">Ps. cx. 11</reference>. It is a debt owing, not to nature, but to God's justice. <hi type="italic">After death the judgment,</hi> and that is a <hi type="italic">day of wrath,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.6.17">Rev. vi. 17</reference>. 2. Riches will stand men in no stead that day. They will neither put by the stroke nor ease the pain, much less take out the sting; what profit will this world's birth-rights be of then? In the day of public judgments riches often expose men rather than protect them, <reference osisRef="Ezek.7.19">Ezek. vii. 19</reference>. 3. It is righteousness only that will <hi type="italic">deliver from</hi> the evil of <hi type="italic">death.</hi> A good conscience will make death easy, and take off the terror of it; it is the privilege of the righteous only not to be hurt of the second death, and so not much hurt by the first.
entries.8d6620ca3b9a21f2efcf49b82442273be0fa6765: <div eID="gen13644" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13645" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">5</hi> The righteousness of the perfect shall direct his way: but the wicked shall fall by his own wickedness. <hi type="super">6</hi> The righteousness of the upright shall deliver them: but transgressors shall be taken in <hi type="italic">their own</hi> naughtiness. <div eID="gen13645" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13646" type="x-p"/> These two verses are, in effect, the same, and both to the same purport with <reference osisRef="Prov.11.3">v. 3</reference>. For the truths are here of such certainty and weight that they cannot be too often inculcated. Let us govern ourselves by these principles. <div eID="gen13646" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13647" type="x-p"/> I. That the ways of religion are plain and safe, and in them we may enjoy a holy security. A living principle of honesty and grace will be, 1. Our best direction in the right way, in every doubtful case to say to us, <hi type="italic">This is the way, walk in it.</hi> He that acts without a guide looks right on and sees his way before him. 2. Our best deliverance from every false way: <hi type="italic">The righteousness of the upright</hi> shall be armour of proof to them, to deliver them from the allurements of the devil and the world, and from their menaces. <div eID="gen13647" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13648" type="x-p"/> The ways of wickedness are dangerous and destructive: <hi type="italic">The wicked shall fail</hi> into misery and ruin <hi type="italic">by their own wickedness,</hi> and be <hi type="italic">taken in their own naughtiness</hi> as in a snare. <hi type="italic">O Israel! thou hast destroyed thyself.</hi> Their sin will be their punishment; that very thing by which they contrived to shelter themselves will make against them.
entries.a4e75b56ed148e4feaefb175965e7743204e6e6e: <div eID="gen13648" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13649" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> When a wicked man dieth, <hi type="italic">his</hi> expectation shall perish: and the hope of unjust <hi type="italic">men</hi> perisheth. <div eID="gen13649" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13650" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Even wicked men, while they live, may keep up a confident expectation of a happiness when they die, or at least a happiness in this world. The hypocrite has his hope, in which he wraps himself as the spider in her web. The worldling expects great matters from his wealth; he calls it <hi type="italic">goods laid up for many years,</hi> and hopes to take his ease in it and to be merry; but in death their expectation will be frustrated: the worldling must leave this world which he expected to continue in and the hypocrite will come short of that world which he expected to remove to, <reference osisRef="Job.27.8">Job xxvii. 8</reference>. 2. It will be the great aggravation of the misery of wicked people that their hopes will sink into despair just when they expect them to be crowned with fruition. When a godly man dies his expectations are out-done, and all his fears vanish; but when a wicked man dies his expectations are dashed, dashed to pieces; in that very day his thoughts perish with which he had pleased himself, his hopes vanish.
entries.b51090999b9075a4db451eca455938f7439c8f62: <div eID="gen13650" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13651" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> The righteous is delivered out of trouble, and the wicked cometh in his stead. <div eID="gen13651" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13652" type="x-p"/> As always in death, so sometimes in life, the righteous are remarkably favoured and the wicked crossed. 1. Good people are helped out of the distresses which they thought themselves lost in, and their feet are set in a large room, <reference osisRef="Ps.66.12">Ps. lxvi. 12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.34.19">xxxiv. 19</reference>. God has found out a way to deliver his people even when they have despaired and their enemies have triumphed, as if the wilderness had shut them in. 2. The wicked have fallen into the distresses which they thought themselves far from, nay, which they had been instrumental to bring the righteous into, so that they seem to come in their stead, as a ransom for the just. Mordecai is saved from the gallows, Daniel from the lion's den, and Peter from the prison; and their persecutors <hi type="italic">come in their stead.</hi> The Israelites are delivered out of the Red Sea and the Egyptians drowned in it. So precious are the saints in God's eye that he <hi type="italic">gives men for them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.43.3-Isa.43.4">Isa. xliii. 3, 4</reference>.
entries.2734ae9bc4dca213d38a61b9b3545438bf2a4181: <div eID="gen13652" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Common Truths.</title> <div sID="gen13653" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> An hypocrite with <hi type="italic">his</hi> mouth destroyeth his neighbour: but through knowledge shall the just be delivered. <div eID="gen13653" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13654" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. Hypocrisy designing ill. It is not only the murderer with his sword, but the <hi type="italic">hypocrite with his mouth,</hi> that <hi type="italic">destroys his neighbour,</hi> decoying him into sin, or into mischief, by the specious pretences of kindness and good-will. <hi type="italic">Death and life are in the power of the tongue,</hi> but no tongue more fatal than the flattering tongue. 2. Honesty defeating the design and escaping the snare: <hi type="italic">Through knowledge</hi> of the devices of Satan <hi type="italic">shall the just be delivered</hi> from the snares which the hypocrite has laid for him; seducers shall not deceive the elect. By the knowledge of God, and the scriptures, and their own hearts, shall the just be delivered from those that lie in wait to deceive, and so to destroy, <reference osisRef="Rom.16.18-Rom.16.19">Rom. xvi. 18, 19</reference>.
entries.01f10999c0e321716d9ef006165f1b5aa89af0b1: <div eID="gen13654" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13655" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> When it goeth well with the righteous, the city rejoiceth: and when the wicked perish, <hi type="italic">there is</hi> shouting. <hi type="super">11</hi> By the blessing of the upright the city is exalted: but it is overthrown by the mouth of the wicked. <div eID="gen13655" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13656" type="x-p"/> It is here observed, <div eID="gen13656" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13657" type="x-p"/> I. That good men are generally well-beloved by their neighbours, but nobody cares for wicked people. 1. It is true there are some few that are enemies to the righteous, that are prejudiced against God and godliness, and are therefore vexed to see good men in power and prosperity; but all indifferent persons, even those that have no great stock of religion themselves, have a good word for a good man; and therefore <hi type="italic">when it goes well with the righteous,</hi> when they are advanced and put into a capacity of doing good according to their desire, it is so much the better for all about them, and <hi type="italic">the city rejoices.</hi> For the honour and encouragement of virtue, and as it is the accomplishment of the promise of God, we should be glad to see virtuous men prosper in the world, and brought into reputation. 2. Wicked people may perhaps have here and there a well-wisher among those who are altogether such as themselves, but among the generality of their neighbours they get ill-will; they may be feared, but they are not loved, and therefore <hi type="italic">when they perish there is shouting;</hi> every body takes a pleasure in seeing them disgraced and disarmed, removed out of places of trust and power, chased out of the world, and wishes no greater loss may come to the town, the rather because they hope <hi type="italic">the righteous may come in their stead,</hi> as they into trouble instead of the righteous, <reference osisRef="Prov.11.8">v. 8</reference>. Let a sense of honour therefore keep us in the paths of virtue, that we may live desired and die lamented, and not be hissed off the stage, <reference osisRef="Job.27.23">Job xxvii. 23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.52.6">Ps. lii. 6</reference>. <div eID="gen13657" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13658" type="x-p"/> II. That there is good reason for this, because those that are good do good, but (<hi type="italic">as saith the proverb of the ancients) wickedness proceeds from the wicked.</hi> 1. <hi type="italic">Good men are public blessings</hi>—<hi type="italic">Vir bonus est commune bonum. By the blessing of the upright,</hi> the blessings with which they are blessed, which enlarge their sphere of usefulness,—by the blessings with which they bless their neighbours, their advice, their example, their prayers, and all the instances of their serviceableness to the public interest,—by the blessings with which God blesses others for their sake,—by these <hi type="italic">the city is exalted</hi> and made more comfortable to the inhabitants, and more considerable among its neighbours. 2. Wicked men are public nuisances, not only the burdens, but the plagues of their generation. The city is <hi type="italic">overthrown by the mouth of the wicked,</hi> whose evil communications corrupt good manners, are enough to debauch a town, to ruin virtue in it, and bring down the judgments of God upon it.
entries.4433d28b835b80065315960b28cd79d4b15a575e: <div eID="gen13658" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13659" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> He that is void of wisdom despiseth his neighbour: but a man of understanding holdeth his peace. <hi type="super">13</hi> A talebearer revealeth secrets: but he that is of a faithful spirit concealeth the matter. <div eID="gen13659" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13660" type="x-p"/> I. Silence is here recommended as an instance of true friendship, and a preservative of it, and therefore an evidence, 1. Of wisdom: <hi type="italic">A man of understanding,</hi> that has rule over his own spirit, if he be provoked, <hi type="italic">holds his peace,</hi> that he may neither give vent to his passion nor kindle the passion of others by any opprobrious language or peevish reflections. 2. Of sincerity: <hi type="italic">He that is of a faithful spirit,</hi> that is true, not only to his own promise, but to the interest of his friend, <hi type="italic">conceals every matter</hi> which, if divulged, may turn to the prejudice of his neighbour. <div eID="gen13660" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13661" type="x-p"/> II. This prudent friendly concealment is here opposed to two very bad vices of the tongue:—1. Speaking scornfully of a man to his face: <hi type="italic">He that is void of wisdom</hi> discovers his folly by this; he <hi type="italic">despises his neighbour,</hi> calls him <hi type="italic">Raca,</hi> and <hi type="italic">Thou fool,</hi> upon the least provocation, and tramples upon him as not worthy to be set with the dogs of his flock. He undervalues himself who thus undervalues one that is made of the same mould. 2. Speaking spitefully of a man behind his back: <hi type="italic">A tale-bearer,</hi> that carries all the stories he can pick up, true or false, from house to house, to make mischief and sow discord, <hi type="italic">reveals secrets</hi> which he has been entrusted with, and so breaks the laws, and forfeits all the privileges, of friendship and conversation.
entries.1a76db101d9917a1634a0509a56f7d39d6e32a11: <div eID="gen13661" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13662" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">14</hi> Where no counsel <hi type="italic">is,</hi> the people fall: but in the multitude of counsellors <hi type="italic">there is</hi> safety. <div eID="gen13662" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13663" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. The bad omen of a kingdom's ruin: <hi type="italic">Where no counsel is,</hi> no consultation at all, but every thing done rashly, or no prudent consultation for the common good, but only caballing for parties and divided interests, <hi type="italic">the people fall,</hi> crumble into factions, fall to pieces, fall together by the ears, and fall an easy prey to their common enemies. Councils of war are necessary to the operations of war; two eyes see more than one; and mutual advice is in order to mutual assistance. 2. The good presage of a kingdom's prosperity: <hi type="italic">In the multitude of counsellors,</hi> that see their need one of another, and act in concert and with concern for the public welfare, <hi type="italic">there is safety;</hi> for what prudent methods one discerns not another may. In our private affairs we shall often find it to our advantage to advise with many; if they agree in their advice, our way will be the more clear; if they differ, we shall hear what is to be said on all sides, and be the better able to determine.
entries.ac9b7561c4fddfa903d537158f6f170c83a1448c: <div eID="gen13663" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Rewards of Righteousness.</title> <div sID="gen13664" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> He that is surety for a stranger shall smart <hi type="italic">for it:</hi> and he that hateth suretiship is sure. <div eID="gen13664" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13665" type="x-p"/> Here we are taught, 1. In general, that we may not use our estates as we will (he that gave them to us has reserved to himself a power to direct us how we shall use them, for they are not our own; we are but stewards), and further that God in his law consults our interests and teaches us that charity which begins at home, as well as that which must not end there. There is a good husbandry which is good divinity, and a discretion in ordering our affairs which is part of the character of a good man, <reference osisRef="Ps.112.5">Ps. cxii. 5</reference>. Every man must be just to his family, else he is not true to his stewardship. 2. In particular, that we must not enter rashly into suretiship, (1.) Because there is danger of bringing ourselves into trouble by it, and our families too when we are gone: <hi type="italic">He that is surety for a stranger,</hi> for any one that asks him and promises him to be bound for him another time, for one whose person perhaps he knows, and thinks he knows his circumstances, but is mistaken, he <hi type="italic">shall smart for it. Contritione conteretur—he shall be certainly and sadly crushed and broken by it,</hi> and perhaps become a bankrupt. Our Lord Jesus was surety for us when we were strangers, nay, enemies, and he smarted for it; <hi type="italic">it pleased the Lord to bruise him.</hi> (2.) Because he that resolves against all such suretiship keeps upon sure grounds, which a man may do if he take care not to launch out any further into business than his own credit will carry him, so that he needs not ask others to be bound for him.
entries.9074469bf0f710b3a9ee56487195a04cae16e688: <div eID="gen13665" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13666" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">16</hi> A gracious woman retaineth honour: and strong <hi type="italic">men</hi> retain riches. <div eID="gen13666" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13667" type="x-p"/> Here, 1. It is allowed that <hi type="italic">strong men retain riches,</hi> that those who bustle in the world, who are men of spirit and interest, and are able to make their part good against all who stand in their way, are likely to keep what they have and to get more, while those who are weak are preyed upon by all about them. 2. It is taken for granted that <hi type="italic">a gracious woman</hi> is as solicitous to preserve her reputation for wisdom and modesty, humility and courtesy, and all those other graces that are the true ornaments of her sex, as strong men are to secure their estates; and those women who are truly gracious will, in like manner, effectually secure their honour by their prudence and good conduct. <hi type="italic">A gracious woman</hi> is as honourable as a valiant man and her honour is as sure.
entries.68a67dee043807b8991fbc8e53ea60910256aa36: <div eID="gen13667" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13668" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">17</hi> The merciful man doeth good to his own soul: but <hi type="italic">he that is</hi> cruel troubleth his own flesh. <div eID="gen13668" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13669" type="x-p"/> It is a common principle, Every one for himself. <hi type="italic">Proximus egomet mihi—None so near to me as myself.</hi> Now, if this be rightly understood, it will be a reason for the cherishing of gracious dispositions in ourselves and the crucifying of corrupt ones. We are friends or enemies to ourselves, even in respect of present comfort, according as we are or are not governed by religious principles. 1. A <hi type="italic">merciful,</hi> tender, good humoured <hi type="italic">man, does good to his own soul,</hi> makes and keeps himself easy. He has the pleasure of doing his duty, and contributing to the comfort of those that are to him as <hi type="italic">his own soul;</hi> for <hi type="italic">we are members one of another.</hi> He that waters others with his temporal good things shall find that God will water him with his spiritual blessings, which will do the best <hi type="italic">good to his own soul.</hi> See <reference osisRef="Isa.58.7">Isa. lviii. 7</reference>, &c. <hi type="italic">If thou hide not thy eyes from thy own flesh,</hi> but do good to others, as to thyself, if thou do good with thy own soul and <hi type="italic">draw that out to the hungry,</hi> thou wilt do good to thy own soul; for the Lord shall <hi type="italic">satisfy thy soul</hi> and <hi type="italic">make fat thy bones.</hi> Some make it part of the character of a <hi type="italic">merciful man,</hi> that he will make much of himself; that disposition which inclines him to be charitable to others will oblige him to allow himself also that which is convenient and to <hi type="italic">enjoy the good of all his labour.</hi> We may by the <hi type="italic">soul</hi> understand the <hi type="italic">inward man,</hi> as the apostle calls it, and then it teaches us that the first and great act of mercy is to provide well for our own souls the necessary supports of the spiritual life. 2. A <hi type="italic">cruel,</hi> froward, ill-natured man, <hi type="italic">troubles his own flesh,</hi> and so his sin becomes his punishment; he starves and dies for want of what he has, because he has not a heart to use it either for the good of others of for his own. He is vexatious to his nearest relations, that are, and should be, to him as his own flesh, <reference osisRef="Eph.5.29">Eph. v. 29</reference>. Envy, and malice, and greediness of the world, are the rottenness of the bones and the consumption of the flesh.
entries.d2c433a3033c08016ffa79593b3244bb240bda66: <div eID="gen13669" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13670" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">18</hi> The wicked worketh a deceitful work: but to him that soweth righteousness <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> a sure reward. <div eID="gen13670" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13671" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Sinners put a most fatal cheat upon themselves: <hi type="italic">The wicked works a deceitful work,</hi> builds himself a house upon the sand, which will deceive him when the storm comes, promises himself <hi type="italic">that</hi> by his sin which he will never gain; nay, it is cutting his throat when it smiles upon him. <hi type="italic">Sin deceived me, and by it slew me.</hi> 2. Saints lay up the best securities for themselves: He <hi type="italic">that sows righteousness,</hi> that is good, and makes it his business to do good, with an eye to a future recompence, he shall have <hi type="italic">a sure reward;</hi> it is made as sure to him as eternal truth can make it. If the seedness fail not, the harvest shall not, <reference osisRef="Gal.6.8">Gal. vi. 8</reference>.
entries.b8ddb92820ab433fbdb0bb3edb279ac00474de27: <div eID="gen13671" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13672" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">19</hi> As righteousness <hi type="italic">tendeth</hi> to life: so he that pursueth evil <hi type="italic">pursueth it</hi> to his own death. <div eID="gen13672" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13673" type="x-p"/> It is here shown that righteousness, not only by the divine judgment, will end in life, and wickedness in death, but that righteousness, in its own nature, has a direct tendency to life and wickedness to death. 1. True holiness is true happiness; it is a preparative for it, a pledge and earnest of it. <hi type="italic">Righteousness</hi> inclines, disposes, and leads, the soul <hi type="italic">to life.</hi> 2. In like manner, those that indulge themselves in sin are fitting themselves for destruction. The more violent a man is in sinful pursuits the more eagerly bent he is upon his own destruction; he awakens it when it seemed to slumber and hastens it when it seemed to linger. <div eID="gen13673" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Weighty Sayings.</title> <div sID="gen13674" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">20</hi> They that are of a froward heart <hi type="italic">are</hi> abomination to the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : but <hi type="italic">such as are</hi> upright in <hi type="italic">their</hi> way <hi type="italic">are</hi> his delight. <div eID="gen13674" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13675" type="x-p"/> It concerns us to know what God hates and what he loves, that we may govern ourselves accordingly, may avoid his displeasure and recommend ourselves to his favour. Now here we are told, 1. That nothing is more offensive to God than hypocrisy and double-dealing, for these are signified by the word which we translate <hi type="italic">frowardness,</hi> pretending justice, but intending wrong, walking in crooked ways, to avoid discovery. Those <hi type="italic">are of a froward heart</hi> who act in contradiction to that which is good, under a profession of that which is good, and such are, more than any sinners, an <hi type="italic">abomination to the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.65.5">Isa. lxv. 5</reference>. 2. That nothing is more pleasing to God than sincerity and plain-dealing: <hi type="italic">Such as are upright in their way,</hi> such as aim and act with integrity, such as have their conversation in the world <hi type="italic">in simplicity and godly sincerity, not with fleshly wisdom,</hi> these God delights in, these he even boasts of (<hi type="italic">Hast thou considered my servant Job?</hi>) and will have us to admire. <hi type="italic">Behold an Israelite indeed!</hi>
entries.6a37088875808b6b5b6305cd6835f776f0420412: <div eID="gen13675" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13676" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">21</hi> <hi type="italic">Though</hi> hand <hi type="italic">join</hi> in hand, the wicked shall not be unpunished: but the seed of the righteous shall be delivered. <div eID="gen13676" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13677" type="x-p"/> Observe, 1. That confederacies in sin shall certainly be broken, and shall not avail to protect the sinners: <hi type="italic">Though hand join in hand,</hi> though there are many that concur by their practice to keep wickedness in countenance, and engage to stand by one another in defending it against all the attacks of virtue and justice,—though they are in league for the support and propagation of it,—though wicked children tread in the steps of their wicked parents, and resolve to keep up the trade, in defiance of religion,—yet all this will not protect them from the justice of God; they shall not be held guiltless; it will not excuse them to say that they did as the most did and as their company did; they <hi type="italic">shall not be unpunished;</hi> witness the flood that was brought upon a whole world of ungodly men. Their number, and strength, and unanimity in sin will stand them in no stead when the day of vengeance comes. 2. That entails of religion shall certainly be blessed: <hi type="italic">The seed of the righteous,</hi> that follow the steps of their righteousness, though they may fall into trouble, shall, in due time, <hi type="italic">be delivered.</hi> Though justice may come slowly to punish the wicked, and mercy may come slowly to save the righteous, yet both will come surely. Sometimes <hi type="italic">the seed of the righteous,</hi> though they are not themselves righteous, are delivered for the sake of their godly ancestors, as Israel often, and the seed of David.
entries.be99d1a49e4d7cdf3f1f53d585bdb493df58db8e: <div eID="gen13677" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13678" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">22</hi> <hi type="italic">As</hi> a jewel of gold in a swine's snout, <hi type="italic">so is</hi> a fair woman which is without discretion. <div eID="gen13678" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13679" type="x-p"/> By <hi type="italic">discretion</hi> here we must understand <hi type="italic">religion</hi> and <hi type="italic">grace,</hi> a true taste and relish (so the word signifies) of the honours and pleasures that attend an unspotted virtue; so that <hi type="italic">a woman without discretion</hi> is a woman of a loose and dissolute conversation; and then observe, 1. It is taken for granted here that beauty or comeliness of body is <hi type="italic">as a jewel of gold,</hi> a thing very valuable, and, where there is wisdom and grace to guard against the temptations of it, it is a great ornament, (<hi type="italic">Gratior est pulchro veniens de corpore virtus—Virtue appears peculiarly graceful when associated with beauty</hi>); but a foolish wanton woman, of a light carriage, is fitly compared to a swine, though she be ever so handsome, wallowing in the mire of filthy lusts, with which the mind and conscience are defiled, and, though washed, returning to them. 2. It is lamented that beauty should be so abused as it is by those that have not modesty with it. It seems ill-bestowed upon them; it is quite misplaced, <hi type="italic">as a jewel in a swine's snout,</hi> with which he roots in the dunghill. If beauty be not guarded by virtue, the virtue is exposed by the beauty. It may be applied to all other bodily endowments and accomplishments; it is a pity that those should have them who have not discretion to use them well.
entries.fdd9cb84f5530c80c94ae2d973a66c5c466c0dbd: <div eID="gen13679" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13680" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">23</hi> The desire of the righteous <hi type="italic">is</hi> only good: <hi type="italic">but</hi> the expectation of the wicked <hi type="italic">is</hi> wrath. <div eID="gen13680" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13681" type="x-p"/> This tells us what <hi type="italic">the desire</hi> and <hi type="italic">expectation of the righteous</hi> and <hi type="italic">of the wicked</hi> are and how they will prove, what they would have and what they shall have. 1. <hi type="italic">The righteous</hi> would have <hi type="italic">good, only good;</hi> all they desire is that it may go well with all about them; they wish no hurt to any, but happiness to all; as to themselves, their desire is not to gratify any evil lust, but to obtain the favour of a good God and to preserve the peace of a good conscience; and good they shall have, that good which they desire, <reference osisRef="Ps.37.4">Ps. xxxvii. 4</reference>. 2. <hi type="italic">The wicked</hi> would have <hi type="italic">wrath;</hi> they desire the woeful day, that God's judgments may gratify their passion and revenge, may remove those that stand in their way, and that they may make an advantage to themselves by fishing in troubled waters; and wrath they shall have, so shall their doom be. They expect and desire mischief to others, but it shall return upon themselves; as they loved cursing, they shall have enough of it.
entries.b9e4444fa98541a2c88001a9fd941f28d205f486: <div eID="gen13681" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Praise of Liberality.</title> <div sID="gen13682" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">24</hi> There is that scattereth, and yet increaseth; and <hi type="italic">there is</hi> that withholdeth more than is meet, but <hi type="italic">it tendeth</hi> to poverty. <div eID="gen13682" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13683" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. It is possible a man may grow rich by prudently spending what he has, may scatter in works of piety, charity, and generosity, and yet may increase; nay, by that means may increase, as the corn is increased by being sown. By cheerfully using what we have our spirits are exhilarated, and so fitted for the business we have to do, by minding which closely what we have is increased; it gains a reputation which contributes to the increase. But it is especially to be ascribed to God; he blesses the giving hand, and so makes it a getting hand, <reference osisRef="2Cor.9.20">2 Cor. ix. 20</reference>. <hi type="italic">Give, and it shall be given you.</hi> 2. It is possible a man may grow poor by meanly sparing what he has, <hi type="italic">withholding more than is meet,</hi> not paying just debts, not relieving the poor, not providing what is convenient for the family, not allowing necessary expenses for the preservation of the goods; this <hi type="italic">tends to poverty;</hi> it cramps men's ingenuity and industry, weakens their interest, destroys their credit, and forfeits the blessing of God: and, let men be ever so saving of what they have, if God blast it and blow upon it, it comes to nothing. <hi type="italic">A fire not blown</hi> shall <hi type="italic">consume it,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hag.1.6">Hag. i. 6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hag.1.9">9</reference>.
entries.735383163fcfcd0c209ee3064c6fe2404b716e5b: <div eID="gen13683" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13684" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">25</hi> The liberal soul shall be made fat: and he that watereth shall be watered also himself. <div eID="gen13684" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13685" type="x-p"/> So backward we are to works of charity, and so ready to think that giving undoes us, that we need to have it very much pressed upon us how much it is for our own advantage to do good to others, as before, <reference osisRef="Prov.11.17">v. 17</reference>. 1. We shall have the comfort of it in our own bosoms: <hi type="italic">The liberal soul,</hi> the soul of blessing, that prays for the afflicted and provides for them, that scatters blessings with gracious lips and generous hands, that soul <hi type="italic">shall be made fat</hi> with true pleasure and enriched with more grace. 2. We shall have the recompence of it both from God and man: <hi type="italic">He that waters</hi> others with the streams of his bounty <hi type="italic">shall be also watered himself;</hi> God will certainly return it in the dews, in the plentiful showers, of his blessing, which he will <hi type="italic">pour out, till there be not room enough to receive it,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mal.3.10">Mal. iii. 10</reference>. Men that have any sense of gratitude will return it if there be occasion; the <hi type="italic">merciful shall find mercy</hi> and the kind be kindly dealt with. 3. We shall be enabled still to do yet more good: <hi type="italic">He that waters, even he shall be as rain</hi> (so some read it); he shall be recruited as the clouds are which return after the rain, and shall be further useful and acceptable, as the rain to the new-mown grass. <hi type="italic">He that teaches shall learn</hi> (so the Chaldee reads it); he that uses his knowledge in teaching others shall himself be taught of God; to him that has, and uses what he has, more shall be given.
entries.f3c817038ca6d8ccddf29060d2acaa4fedbab2e3: <div eID="gen13685" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13686" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">26</hi> He that withholdeth corn, the people shall curse him: but blessing <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> upon the head of him that selleth <hi type="italic">it.</hi> <div eID="gen13686" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13687" type="x-p"/> See here, 1. What use we are to make of the gifts of God's bounty; we must not hoard them up merely for our own advantage, that we may be enriched by them, but we must bring them forth for the benefit of others, that they may be supported and maintained by them. It is a sin, when corn is dear and scarce, to withhold it, in hopes that it will still grow dearer, so to keep up and advance the market, when it is already so high that the poor suffer by it; and at such a time it is the duty of those that have stocks of corn by them to consider the poor, and to be willing to sell at the market-price, to be content with moderate profit, and not aim to make a gain of God's judgments. It is a noble and extensive piece of charity for those that have stores wherewithal to do it to help to keep the markets low when the price of our commodities grows excessive. 2. What regard we are to have to the voice of the people. We are not to think it an indifferent thing, and not worth heeding, whether we have the ill will and word, or the good will and word, of our neighbours, their prayers or their curses; for here we are taught to dread their curses, and forego our own profit rather than incur them; and to court their blessings, and be at some expense to purchase them. Sometimes, <hi type="italic">vox populi est vox Dei</hi>—<hi type="italic">the voice of the people is the voice of God.</hi>
entries.bee2257824560c6d192b73e3817d14a9060d79ff: <div eID="gen13687" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Folly and Misery of Sinners.</title> <div sID="gen13688" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">27</hi> He that diligently seeketh good procureth favour: but he that seeketh mischief, it shall come unto him. <div eID="gen13688" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13689" type="x-p"/> Observe, 1. Those that are industrious to do good in the world get themselves beloved both with God and man: <hi type="italic">He that rises early to that which is good</hi> (so the word is), that seeks opportunities of serving his friends and relieving the poor, and lays out himself therein, <hi type="italic">procures favour.</hi> All about him love him, and speak well of him, and will be ready to do him a kindness; and, which is better than that, better than life, he has God's lovingkindness. 2. Those that are industrious to do mischief are preparing ruin for themselves: <hi type="italic">It shall come unto them;</hi> some time or other they will be paid in their own coin. And, observe, <hi type="italic">seeking mischief</hi> is here set in opposition to <hi type="italic">seeking good;</hi> for those that are not doing good are doing hurt.
entries.bc21b7913f66fc0ab90612a690610200dc6f4f51: <div eID="gen13689" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13690" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">28</hi> He that trusteth in his riches shall fall: but the righteous shall flourish as a branch. <div eID="gen13690" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13691" type="x-p"/> Observe, 1. Our riches will fail us when we are in the greatest need: <hi type="italic">He that trusts in them,</hi> as if they would secure him the favour of God and be his protection and portion, <hi type="italic">shall fall,</hi> as a man who lays his weight on a broken reed, which will not only disappoint him, but run into his hand and pierce him. 2. Our righteousness will stand us in stead when our riches fail us: <hi type="italic">The righteous shall</hi> then <hi type="italic">flourish as a branch,</hi> the branch of righteousness, like a tree whose leaf shall not wither, <reference osisRef="Ps.1.3">Ps. i. 3</reference>. Even in death, when riches fail men, the <hi type="italic">bones</hi> of the righteous <hi type="italic">shall flourish as a herb,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.66.14">Isa. lxvi. 14</reference>. When those that take root in the world wither those that are grafted into Christ and partake of his root and fatness shall be fruitful and flourishing.
entries.9214f6c968bcfd20e1feeb937385314c61aa6bec: <div eID="gen13691" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13692" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">29</hi> He that troubleth his own house shall inherit the wind: and the fool <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> servant to the wise of heart. <div eID="gen13692" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13693" type="x-p"/> Two extremes in the management of family-affairs are here condemned and the ill consequences of them foretold:—1. Carefulness and carnal policy, on the one hand. There are those that by their extreme earnestness in pursuit of the world, their anxiety about their business and fretfulness about their losses, their strictness with their servants and their niggardliness towards their families, <hi type="italic">trouble their own houses</hi> and give continual vexation to all about them; while others think, by supporting factions and feuds in their families, which are really a trouble to their houses, to serve some turn for themselves, and either to get or to save by it. But they will both be disappointed; they will <hi type="italic">inherit the wind.</hi> All they will get by these arts will not only be empty and worthless as the wind, but noisy and troublesome, vanity and vexation. 2. Carelessness and want of common prudence, on the other. He that is a fool in his business, that either minds it not or goes awkwardly about it, that has no contrivance and consideration, no only loses his reputation and interest, but becomes a <hi type="italic">servant to the wise in heart.</hi> He is impoverished, and forced to work for his living; while those that manage wisely raise themselves, and come to have dominion over him, and others like him. It is rational, and very fit, that <hi type="italic">the fool</hi> should <hi type="italic">be servant to the wise in heart,</hi> and upon that account, among others, we are bound to submit our wills to the will of God, and to be subject to him, because we are fools and he is infinitely wise.
entries.79c59ce30c99578f629363f284f8d6fbfa54f30a: <div eID="gen13693" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13694" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">30</hi> The fruit of the righteous <hi type="italic">is</hi> a tree of life; and he that winneth souls <hi type="italic">is</hi> wise. <div eID="gen13694" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13695" type="x-p"/> This shows what great blessings good men are, especially those that are eminently wise, to the places where they live, and therefore how much to be valued. 1. The righteous are as <hi type="italic">trees of life;</hi> the fruits of their piety and charity, their instructions, reproofs, examples, and prayers, their interest in heaven, and their influence upon earth, are like the fruits of that tree, precious and useful, contributing to the support and nourishment of the spiritual life in many; they are the ornaments of paradise, God's church on earth, for whose sake it stands. 2. The wise are something more; they are as trees of knowledge, not forbidden, but commanded knowledge. <hi type="italic">He that is wise,</hi> by communicating his wisdom, <hi type="italic">wins souls,</hi> wins upon them to bring them in love with God and holiness, and so wins them over into the interests of God's kingdom among men. The wise are said to <hi type="italic">turn many to righteousness,</hi> and that is the same with winning souls here, <reference osisRef="Dan.12.3">Dan. xii. 3</reference>. Abraham's proselytes are called <hi type="italic">the souls that he had gotten,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.12.5">Gen. xii. 5</reference>. Those that would win souls have need of wisdom to know how to deal with them; and those that do win souls show that they are wise.
entries.372f451be747f8835db86aa5ac608f67cef262d8: <div eID="gen13695" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13696" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">31</hi> Behold, the righteous shall be recompensed in the earth: much more the wicked and the sinner. <div eID="gen13696" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13697" type="x-p"/> This, I think, is the only one of Solomon's proverbs that has that note of attention prefixed to it, <hi type="italic">Behold!</hi> which intimates that it contains not only an evident truth, which may be beheld, but an eminent truth, which must be considered. 1. Some understand both parts of a recompence in displeasure: <hi type="italic">The righteous,</hi> if they do amiss, shall be punished for their offences in this world; much more shall wicked people be punished for theirs, which are committed, not through infirmity, but with a high hand. If judgment begin at the house of God, what will become of the ungodly? <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.17-1Pet.4.18">1 Pet. iv. 17, 18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.23.31">Luke xxiii. 31</reference>. 2. I rather understand it of a recompence of reward to the righteous and punishment to sinners. Let us behold providential retributions. There are some recompences <hi type="italic">in the earth,</hi> in this world, and in the things of this world, which prove that <hi type="italic">verily there is a God that judges in the earth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.58.11">Ps. lviii. 11</reference>); but they are not universal; many sins go unpunished in the earth, and services unrewarded, which indicates that there is a judgment to come, and that there will be more exact and full retributions in the future state. Many times <hi type="italic">the righteous</hi> are <hi type="italic">recompensed</hi> for their righteousness here <hi type="italic">in the earth,</hi> though that is not the principal, much less the only reward either intended for them or intended by them; but whatever the word of God has promised them, or the wisdom of God sees good for them, they shall have <hi type="italic">in the earth. The wicked</hi> also, <hi type="italic">and the sinner,</hi> are sometimes remarkably punished in this life, nations, families, particular persons. And if the righteous, who do not deserve the least reward, yet have part of their recompence here on earth, much more shall the wicked, who deserve the greatest punishment, have part of their punishment on earth, as an earnest of worse to come. Therefore <hi type="italic">stand in awe and sin not.</hi> If those have two heavens that merit none, much more shall those have two hells that merit both.  <chapter eID="Prov.11"/> <div eID="gen13697" type="x-p"/>

entries.18dfccde93c133536197c820f3d80938b9be0389: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7407"/><div sID="gen11445" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7407"/><hi type="bold">5. direct--</hi>or, "make plain"; wicked ways are not plain (<reference osisRef="Prov.13.17">Pr 13:17</reference>). <div eID="gen11445" type="x-p"/>
entries.98a77cb1ec25d18239e2c491edece42016013225: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7408"/><div sID="gen11446" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7408"/><hi type="bold">6. deliver them--</hi>that is, from evil, which the wicked suffer by their own doings (<reference osisRef="Prov.5.22">Pr 5:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.9.16">Psa 9:16</reference>). <div eID="gen11446" type="x-p"/>

entries.99b04c9cd4d63916a0f5ea0d608d33ba35afa5ec: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7414"/><div sID="gen11453" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7414"/><hi type="bold">12. despiseth--</hi>or, "reviles," a course contrasted with the prudent silence of the wise.<div eID="gen11453" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11454" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">holdeth his peace--</hi>as if neither hearing nor telling. <div eID="gen11454" type="x-p"/>
entries.94cc13cde0781da8013400aadda35991c9489eee: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7415"/><div sID="gen11455" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7415"/><hi type="bold">13. tale-bearer--</hi>(Compare Margin), one trading as a peddler in scandal, whose propensity to talk leads him to betray confidence. <div eID="gen11455" type="x-p"/>

entries.016ecb2371f0d64141924c64f7a6f674e7c41bdd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7418"/><div sID="gen11460" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7418"/><hi type="bold">16. retaineth--</hi>or literally, "lay hold of as a support." entries.f4c3ac346d460d0d8de0efea47f4675a584e8f4c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7419"/><div sID="gen11461" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7419"/><hi type="bold">17. merciful--</hi>kind to others; opposed to cruel. Such benefit themselves by doing good to others (compare <reference osisRef="Prov.24.5">Pr 24:5</reference>), while the cruel injure themselves as well as others.<div eID="gen11461" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11462" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">flesh--</hi>that is, his body, by penuriousness (<reference osisRef="Col.2.23">Col 2:23</reference>). <div eID="gen11462" type="x-p"/>
entries.fbd077e4ac687006587df6271e4adb6fd5a59dd7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7420"/><div sID="gen11463" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7420"/><hi type="bold">18. a deceitful work--</hi>or, "wages," which fail to satisfy, or flee away (<reference osisRef="Prov.10.2">Pr 10:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.23.5">23:5</reference>).<div eID="gen11463" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11464" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sure reward--</hi>or, "gain," as from trading (<reference osisRef="Hos.10.12">Ho 10:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.6.8">Ga 6:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gal.6.9">9</reference>). <div eID="gen11464" type="x-p"/>
entries.46465681d5725b9ca14c2eb2c749919b3c6485d8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7421"/><div sID="gen11465" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7421"/>19. entries.2bdc7ea45f9735d9752622007579f8aa82676a4e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7422"/><div sID="gen11466" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7422"/>20. (Compare <reference osisRef="Prov.11.5">Pr 11:5</reference>).<div eID="gen11466" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11467" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">froward--</hi>as in <reference osisRef="Prov.2.15">Pr 2:15</reference>, opposed to the simplicity and purity of the upright.<div eID="gen11467" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11468" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in their way--</hi>or, "conduct." <div eID="gen11468" type="x-p"/>
entries.c2f64ad6fbdf6d93be0aa3a4ce1b74d1adcf85e6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7423"/><div sID="gen11469" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7423"/>21. The combined power of the wicked cannot free them from just punishment, while the unaided children of the righteous find deliverance by reason of their pious relationship (<reference osisRef="Ps.37.25">Psa 37:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.37.26">26</reference>). <div eID="gen11469" type="x-p"/>
entries.539bb3c119bdc814da77b4030560d8fcd048eb3b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7424"/><div sID="gen11470" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7424"/>22. Jewels were often suspended from the nose (<reference osisRef="Gen.24.47">Ge 24:47</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.3.21">Is 3:21</reference>). Thus adorned, a hog disgusts less than a fair and indiscreet woman. <div eID="gen11470" type="x-p"/>
entries.83b12ad10257750f628fad0e9151fb5db0cea189: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7425"/><div sID="gen11471" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7425"/>23. (Compare <reference osisRef="Prov.10.28">Pr 10:28</reference>).<div eID="gen11471" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11472" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wrath--</hi>is that of God. <div eID="gen11472" type="x-p"/>
entries.f0f73827372ca59a24ebfc38ba587f7987eb5461: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7426"/><div sID="gen11473" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7426"/>24-31. entries.8ff4716ae8caf62aada2debcf00159b616486305: <div eID="gen24126" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen24127" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen24128" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen24128" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen24127" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen24129" type="x-p"/> A parallel of the advantages of the righteous and wise, opposed to the miseries of the wicked and the foolish. True and false riches. <div eID="gen24129" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24130" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen24130" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24131" type="x-p"/> A false balance is abomination - This refers to the balance itself deceitfully constructed, so that it is sooner turned at one end than at the other. This is occasioned by one end of the beam being longer than the other. <div eID="gen24131" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24132" type="x-p"/> But a just weight - אבן שלמה eben shelemah, the perfect stone probably because weights were first made of stone; see the law, <reference osisRef="Deu.25.13-Deu.25.16">Deu 25:13-16</reference> (note).
entries.5369827a5d736d583eb25f0a7da05a4386d9a396: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen24132" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24133" type="x-p"/> When pride cometh - The proud man thinks much more of himself than any other can do; and, expecting to be treated according to his own supposed worth, which treatment he seldom meets with, he is repeatedly mortified, ashamed, confounded, and rendered indignant. <div eID="gen24133" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24134" type="x-p"/> With the lowly - צנועים tsenuim, ταπεινων, the humble, the modest, as opposed to the proud, referred to in the first clause. The humble man looks for nothing but justice; has the meanest opinion of himself; expects nothing in the way of commendation or praise; and can never be disappointed but in receiving praise, which he neither expects nor desires.
entries.e16ee529ae578aec1c90a538618c3c7d14a5c246: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen24134" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24135" type="x-p"/> Riches profit not in the day of wrath - Among men they can do all things; but they cannot purchase the remission of sins, nor turn aside the wrath of God when that is poured out upon the opulent transgressor.
entries.c6723bb4fa36d648f48c288031cc9f66a5c0c591: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen24135" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24136" type="x-p"/> When a wicked man dieth - Hope is a great blessing to man in his present state of trial and suffering; because it leads him to expect a favorable termination of his ills. But hope was not made for the wicked; and yet they are the very persons that most abound in it! They hope to be saved, and get at last to the kingdom of God; though they have their face towards perdition, and refuse to turn. But their hope goes no farther than the grave. There the wicked man's expectation is cut off, and his hope perishes. But to the saint, the penitent, and the cross-bearers in general, what a treasure is hope! What a balm through life!
entries.9a100721f88362fba6aa28c8cc40444e166d9ae8: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen24136" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24137" type="x-p"/> The wicked cometh in his stead - Often God makes this distinction; in public calamities and in sudden accidents he rescues the righteous, and leaves the wicked, who has filled up the measure of his iniquities, to be seized by the hand of death. Justice, then, does its own work; for mercy has been rejected.
entries.7d05ed53c91f8b68baafba05d7b10cfd607cc790: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen24137" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24138" type="x-p"/> A hypocrite with his mouth - חנף chaneph might be better translated infidel than hypocrite. The latter is one that pretends to religion; that uses it for secular purposes. The former is one who disbelieves Divine revelation, and accordingly is polluted, and lives in pollution. This is properly the force of the original word. Such persons deal in calumny and lies, and often thus destroy the character of their neighbor. Besides, they are very zealous in propagating their own infidel notions; and thus, by this means, destroy their neighbor; but the experimental knowledge which the just have of God and his salvation prevents them from being ensnared.
entries.ed1aa43d8aec6f2ce10af215205eeec011efd229: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen24138" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24139" type="x-p"/> When it goeth well - An upright, pious, sensible man is a great blessing to the neighborhood where he resides, by his example, his advice, and his prayers. The considerate prize him on these accounts, and rejoice in his prosperity. But when the wicked perish, who has been a general curse by the contagion of his example and conversation, there is not only no regret expressed for his decease, but a general joy because God has removed him.
entries.e535356cca22fc21c211cb1cbffc47760f162952: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen24139" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24140" type="x-p"/> He that is void of wisdom - A foolish man is generally abundant in his censures; he dwells on the defects of his neighbor, and is sure to bring them into the most prominent view. But a man of understanding - a prudent, sensible man, hides those defects wherever he can, and puts the most charitable construction on those which he cannot conceal.
entries.641b3ab00647bc397565153b37784fd1418da4c1: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen24140" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24141" type="x-p"/> A talebearer - הולך רכיל holech rachil, the walking busybody, the trader in scandal. <div eID="gen24141" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24142" type="x-p"/> Revealeth secrets - Whatever was confided to him he is sure to publish abroad. The word means a hawker, or travelling chapman. Such are always great newsmongers; and will tell even their own secrets, rather than have nothing to say.
entries.bd987f96106f05653d9bc4031112174a72bc9631: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen24142" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24143" type="x-p"/> He that is surety for a stranger shall smart for it - He shall find evil upon evil in it. See on <reference osisRef="Pro.6.1">Pro 6:1</reference> (note).
entries.535f3dd592386f43b12f5c009d5c6e20fdc633c5: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen24143" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24144" type="x-p"/> A gracious woman retaineth honor - Instead of this clause, the Septuagint have, Γυνη ευχαριστος εγειρει ανδρι δοζαν, "A gracious woman raiseth up honor to the man;" Θρονος δε ατιμιας γυνη μισουσα δικαια, "But she that hateth righteous things is a throne of dishonor." A good wife is an honor to her husband; and a bad wife is her husband's reproach: if this be so, how careful should a man be whom he marries!
entries.2a59c607cb7c985a14b77a239c3dbafbfa680027: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen24144" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24145" type="x-p"/> The merciful man doeth good to his own soul - Every gracious disposition is increased while a man is exercised in showing mercy. No man can show an act of disinterested mercy without benefiting his own soul, by improving his moral feeling. <div eID="gen24145" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24146" type="x-p"/> But he that is cruel troubleth his own flesh - We seldom see a peevish, fretful, vindictive man either in good health, or good plight of body. I have often heard it observed of such, "He frets his flesh off his bones."
entries.7f00e60bdc2430746d6610646c06ef733b865947: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen24146" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24147" type="x-p"/> Worketh a deceitful work - An unstable work; nothing is durable that he does, except his crimes.
entries.194415a1bf4db955eb23c24eea83ac6842d77a5e: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen24147" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24148" type="x-p"/> Righteousness tendeth to life - True godliness promotes health, and is the best means of lengthening out life; but wicked men live not out half their days.
entries.3615928b474dda95477c52865c98af990bfaed95: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen24148" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24149" type="x-p"/> Though hand join in hand - Let them confederate as they please, to support each other, justice will take care that they escape not punishment. The Hindoos sometimes ratify an engagement by one person laying his right hand on the hand of another - Ward.
entries.4b063e8307eccc0980ba9e9ce3864a714f9a0108: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen24149" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24150" type="x-p"/> A jewel of gold in a swine's snout - That is, beauty in a woman destitute of good breeding and modest carriage, is as becoming as a gold ring on the snout of a swine. Coverdale translates thus: "A fayre woman without discrete maners, is like a ringe of golde in a swyne's snoute." In Asiatic countries the nose jewel is very common: to this the text alludes.
entries.b6016c155644ba5889c32343f74dd0b81701f10c: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen24150" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24151" type="x-p"/> There is that scattereth, and yet increaseth - The bountiful man, who gives to the poor, never turning away his face from any one in distress, the Lord blesses his property and the bread is multiplied in his hand. To the same purpose the following verse.
entries.295e42f037ff5f425562d5ebaf7c035af4b62460: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen24151" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24152" type="x-p"/> The liberal soul shall be made fat - He who gives to the distressed, in the true spirit of charity, shall get a hundred fold from God's mercy. How wonderful is the Lord! He gives the property, gives the heart to use it aright, and recompenses the man for the deed though all the fruit was found from himself! <div eID="gen24152" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24153" type="x-p"/> He that watereth - A man who distributes in the right spirit gets more good himself than the poor man does who receives the bounty. Thus it is more blessed to give than to receive.
entries.46a0fb7cb22351b184fd5c502d0b98fc83eb8b3a: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen24153" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24154" type="x-p"/> He that withholdeth corn - Who refuses to sell because he hopes for a dearth, and then he can make his own price. <div eID="gen24154" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24155" type="x-p"/> The people shall curse him - Yes, and God shall curse him also; and if he do not return and repent, he will get God's curse, and the curse of the poor, which will be a canker in his money during time, and in his soul throughout eternity.
entries.22ea6d6a520454aed4aa37db9f0c90215f355f1b: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen24155" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24156" type="x-p"/> Shalt inherit the wind - He who dissipates his property by riotous living, shall be as unsatisfied as he who attempts to feed upon air.
entries.7e491a6905aa7a57bd3b80faa4be708e8a51db09: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen24156" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24157" type="x-p"/> The fruit of the righteous is a tree of life - עץ חיים ets chaiyim, "the tree of lives." It is like that tree which grew in the paradise of God; increasing the bodily and mental vigor of those who ate of it. <div eID="gen24157" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24158" type="x-p"/> He that winneth souls is wise - Wisdom seeks to reclaim the wanderers; and he who is influenced by wisdom will do the same.
entries.1b4a2d1e52a1e74740f79412c3bf17eb914498a1: <hi type="bold">Verse 31</hi> <div eID="gen24158" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24159" type="x-p"/> Behold, the righteous shall be recompensed in the earth, etc. - The Septuagint, Syrian, and Arabic read this verse as follows: "And if the righteous scarcely be saved, where shall the ungodly and the sinner appear?" And this St, Peter quotes literatim, <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.18">1Pet 4:18</reference> (note), where see the note.  <chapter eID="Prov.11"/> <div eID="gen24159" type="x-p"/>

entries.79c1a1cd4e28c5b9100575ec28b59e17c89f1923: <reference osisRef="Prov.11.1">Pro 11:1</reference> <div eID="gen10957" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10958" type="x-p"/> The next three proverbs treat of honesty, discretion, and innocence or dove-like simplicity: 1 Deceitful balances are an abomination to Jahve;    But a full weight is His delight. <div eID="gen10958" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10959" type="x-p"/> The very same proverb, with slightly varied expression, is found in <reference osisRef="Prov.20.23">Pro 20:23</reference>; and other such like proverbs, in condemnation of false and in approbation of true balances, are found, <reference osisRef="Prov.20.10">Pro 20:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.16.11">Pro 16:11</reference>; similar predicates, but connected with other subjects, are found at <reference osisRef="Prov.12.22">Pro 12:22</reference>; Pro 15:8. “An abomination to Jahve” is an expression we have already twice met with in the introduction, <reference osisRef="Prov.3.32">Pro 3:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.6.16">Pro 6:16</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.8.7">Pro 8:7</reference>; תּועבה is, like תּועה, a participial noun, in which the active conception of abhorring is transferred to the action accomplished. רצון is in post-biblical Hebr. the designation of the <hi type="italic">arbitrium</hi> and the <hi type="italic">voluntas</hi>; but here רצונו signifies not that which God wishes, but that which He delights in having. “מרמה (here for the first time in Proverbs), from רמה, the <hi type="italic">Piel</hi> of which means (<reference osisRef="Prov.26.19">Pro 26:19</reference>) <hi type="italic">aliquem dolo et fraude petere</hi>. אבן, like the Pers. sanak, sanakh, Arab. ṣajat, a stone for weight; and finally, without any reference to its root signification, like Zec 5:8, אבן העופרת, a leaden weight, as when we say: a horseshoe of gold, a chess-man of ivory.”
entries.6c6c3482677f8042b1039315b63cf81ecf84924b: <reference osisRef="Prov.11.2">Pro 11:2</reference> <div eID="gen10959" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10960" type="x-p"/> Now follows the Solomonic “Pride goeth before a fall.” <div eID="gen10960" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10961" type="x-p"/> There cometh arrogance, so also cometh shame; <div eID="gen10961" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10962" type="x-p"/> But with the humble is wisdom. <div eID="gen10962" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10963" type="x-p"/> Interpreted according to the Hebr.: if the former has come, so immediately also comes the latter. The general truth as to the causal connection of the two is conceived of historically; the fact, confirmed by many events, is represented in the form of a single occurrence as a warning example; the preterites are like the Greek <hi type="italic">aoristi gnomici</hi> (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., p. 32); and the perf., with the <hi type="italic">fut. consec</hi>. following, is the expression of the immediate and almost simultaneous consequence (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., at <reference osisRef="Hab.3.10">Hab 3:10</reference>): has haughtiness (זדון after the form לצון, from זיד, to boil, to run over) appeared, then immediately also disgrace appeared, in which the arrogant behaviour is overwhelmed. The harmony of the sound of the Hebr. זדון and קלון cannot be reproduced in German [nor in English]; Hitzig and Ewald try to do so, but such a <hi type="italic">quid pro quo</hi> as “<hi type="italic">Kommt Unglimpf kommt an ihn Schimpf</hi>” [there comes arrogance, there comes to him disgrace] is not a translation, but a distortion of the text. If, now, the antithesis says that with the humble is wisdom, wisdom is meant which avoids such disgrace as arrogance draws along with it; for the צנוּע thinks not more highly of himself than he ought to think (R. צן, <hi type="italic">subsidere, demitti</hi>, <hi type="italic">Deutsch. Morgenl. Zeitsch</hi>. xxv. 185).
entries.2aade3f7f25a12a1b27d2c612cea0604991e69ed: <reference osisRef="Prov.11.3">Pro 11:3</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.11.3">3</reference> The integrity of the upright guideth them;    But the perverseness of the ungodly destroyeth them. <div eID="gen10963" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10964" type="x-p"/> To the upright, ישׁרים, who keep the line of rectitude without turning aside therefrom into devious paths (Psa 125:4.), stand opposed (as at Pro 2:21.) the ungodly (faithless), בּגדים, who conceal (from בּגד, to cover, whence בּגד = כּסוּת) malicious thoughts and plans. And the contrast of תּמּה, integrity = unreserved loving submission, is סלף, a word peculiar to the Solomonic Mashal, with its verb סלּף (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., p. 32). Hitzig explains it by the Arab. saraf, to step out, to tread over; and Ewald by lafat, to turn, to turn about (“treacherous, false step”), both of which are improbable. Schultens compares salaf in the meaning to smear (R. לף, לב, ἀλείφειν; cf. regarding such secondary formations with ש preceding, Hupfeld on <reference osisRef="Ps.5.7">Psa 5:7</reference>), and translates here, <hi type="italic">lubricitas</hi>. But this rendering is scarcely admissible. It has against it lexical tradition (Menahem: מוטה, wavering; Perchon: זיוף, falsifying; Kimchi: עוות, misrepresentation, according to which the <hi type="italic">Graec. Venet.</hi> σκολιότης), as well as the methodical comparison of the words. The Syriac has not this verbal stem, but the Targum has סלף in the meaning to distort, to turn the wrong way (σκολιοῦν, στρεβλοῦν), <reference osisRef="Prov.10.10">Pro 10:10</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Esth.6.10">Est 6:10</reference>, where, in the second Targum, פּוּמהּ אסתּלף means “his mouth was crooked.” With justice, therefore, Gesenius in his <hi type="italic">Thesaurus</hi> has decided in favour of the fundamental idea <hi type="italic">pervertere</hi>, from which also the Peshito and Saadia proceed; for in <reference osisRef="Exod.23.8">Exo 23:8</reference> they translate (Syr.) mhapêk (it, the gift of bribery, perverts) and (Arab.) tazyf (= תּזיּף, it falsifies). Fl. also, who at <reference osisRef="Prov.15.4">Pro 15:4</reference> remarks, “סלף, from סלף, to stir up, to turn over, so that the lowermost becomes the uppermost,” gives the preference to this primary idea, in view of the Arab. salaf, <hi type="italic">invertere terram conserendi causa</hi>. It is moreover confirmed by salaf, <hi type="italic">praecedere</hi>, which is <hi type="italic">pervertere</hi> modified to <hi type="italic">praevertere</hi>. But how does סלף mean <hi type="italic">perversio</hi> (Theod. ὑποσκελισμός), in the sense of the overthrow prepared for thy neighbour? The parallels demand the sense of a condition peculiar to the word and conduct of the godless (treacherous), <reference osisRef="Prov.22.12">Pro 22:12</reference> (cf. <reference osisRef="Exod.23.8">Exo 23:8</reference>), <reference osisRef="Prov.19.3">Pro 19:3</reference>, thus <hi type="italic">perversitas</hi>, perversity; but this as contrary to truth and rectitude (opp. תּמּה), “perverseness,” as we have translated it, for we understand by it want of rectitude (dishonesty) and untruthfulness. While the sincerity of the upright conducts them, and, so to say, forms their <hi type="italic">salvus conductus</hi>, which guards them against the danger of erring and of hostile assault, the perverseness of the treacherous destroys them; for the disfiguring of truth avenges itself against them, and they experience the reverse of the proverb, “<hi type="italic">das Ehrlich währt am längsten</hi>” (honesty endures the longest). The Chethı̂b ושׁדם (ושׁדּם) is an error of transcription; the Kerı̂ has the proper correction, ישׁדּם = ישׁדדם, Jer 5:6. Regarding שׁדד (whence שׁדּי), which, from its root-signification of making close and fast, denotes violence and destruction, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., under Gen 17.
entries.b695c29edfcee663ae012613447ede6a9095ec01: <reference osisRef="Prov.11.4">Pro 11:4</reference> <div eID="gen10964" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10965" type="x-p"/> Three proverbs in praise of צדקה: 4 Possessions are of no profit in the day of wrath;    But righteousness delivereth from death. <div eID="gen10965" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10966" type="x-p"/> That which is new here, is only that possessions and goods (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., regarding הון, p. 63) are destitute of all value in the day of the μέλλουσα ὀργή; for יום עברה, the day of wrath breaking through the limits (of long-suffering), has the same meaning as in the prophets; and such prophetic words as <reference osisRef="Isa.10.3">Isa 10:3</reference>; Zep 1:18, and, almost in the same words, <reference osisRef="Ezek.7.19">Eze 7:19</reference>, are altogether similar to this proverb. The lxx, which translates ἐν ήμέρᾳ ἐπαγωγῆς, harmonizes in expression with Sir. 5:8, cf. 2:2. Theodotion translates איד, <reference osisRef="Prov.27.10">Pro 27:10</reference>, by ἐπαγωγή (providence, fate).
entries.bb8bbefa770b0ebc7f73f3a7088a4b3495f81b55: <reference osisRef="Prov.11.5">Pro 11:5</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.11.5">5</reference> The righteousness of the blameless smootheth his way,    And by his own wickedness doth the wicked fall. <div eID="gen10966" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10967" type="x-p"/> With the תּמים (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.1.12">Pro 1:12</reference>), formed after the passive, more than with תּם, is connected the idea of the perfected, but more in the negative sense of moral spotlessness than of moral perfection. The rectitude of a man who seeks to keep his conscience and his character pure, maketh smooth (ישּׁר, as <reference osisRef="Prov.3.6">Pro 3:6</reference>, not of the straightness of the line, but of the surface, evenness) his life’s path, so that he can pursue his aim without stumbling and hindrance, and swerving from the direct way; while, on the contrary, the godless comes to ruin by his godlessness - that by which he seeks to forward his interests, and to make a way for himself, becomes his destruction.
entries.affdb54f8eb09ae03de2d6a6afa9a08f88174f12: <reference osisRef="Prov.11.6">Pro 11:6</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.11.6">6</reference> The rectitude of the upright saveth them,    And in their own covetousness are the faithless taken. <div eID="gen10967" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10968" type="x-p"/> The integrity of those who go straight forward and straight through, without permitting themselves to turn aside on crooked ways, delivers them from the snares which are laid for them, the dangers they encounter; while, on the contrary, the faithless, though they mask their intentions ever so cunningly, are ensnared in their passionate covetousness: the mask is removed, they are convicted, and are caught and lost. Regarding הוּה, abyss, overthrow, also stumbling against anything = covetousness, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., at <reference osisRef="Prov.10.3">Pro 10:3</reference>, and under Psa 5:10. The form of the expression 6b follows the scheme, “in the image of God created He man,” Gen 9:6. The subject is to be taken from the genitive, as is marked by the accentuation, for it gives <hi type="italic">Mugrash</hi> to the וּבהוּת, as if it were the principal form, for וּבהוּה.
entries.923b121b8bd6fbe7390e369e28d4d7f63c894df6: <reference osisRef="Prov.11.7">Pro 11:7</reference> <div eID="gen10968" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10969" type="x-p"/> Three proverbs regarding destruction and salvation: 7 When a godless man dies, his hope cometh to nought,    And the expectation of those who stand in fulness of strength is destroyed. <div eID="gen10969" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10970" type="x-p"/> We have already remarked in the Introduction that אדם is a favourite word of the <hi type="italic">Chokma</hi>, and the terminological distinction of different classes and properties of men (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., pp. 40, 42); we read, <reference osisRef="Prov.6.12">Pro 6:12</reference>, אדם בּליּעל, and here, as also <reference osisRef="Job.20.29">Job 20:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.27.13">Job 27:13</reference>, אדם רשׁע, cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.21.29">Pro 21:29</reference>, אישׁ רשׁע, but generally only רשׁע is used. A godless man, to whom earthly possessions and pleasure and honour are the highest good, and to whom no means are too base, in order that he may appease this his threefold passion, rocks himself in unbounded and measureless hopes; but with his death, his hope, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, all that he hoped for, comes to nought. The lxx translate τελευτήσαντος ἀνδρὸς δικαίου οὐκ ὄλλυται ἐλπίς, which is the converse of that which is here said, 7a: the hope of the righteous expects its fulfilment beyond the grave. The lxx further translate, τὸ δὲ καύχημα (וּתהלּת) τῶν ἀσεβῶν ὄλλυται; but the distich in the Hebr. text is not an antithetic one, and whether אונים may signify the wicked (thus also the Syr., Targ., <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>., and Luther), if we regard it as a brachyology for אנשׁי אונים, or as the plur. of an adj. און, after the form טוב (Elazar b. Jacob in Kimchi), or wickedness (Zöckler, with Hitzig, “the wicked expectation”), is very questionable. Yet more improbable is Malbim’s (with Rashi’s) rendering of this אונים, after <reference osisRef="Gen.49.3">Gen 49:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.78.51">Psa 78:51</reference>, and the Targ. on <reference osisRef="Job.18.12">Job 18:12</reference>, of the children of the deceased; children <hi type="italic">gignuntur ex robore virili</hi>, but are not themselves the <hi type="italic">robur virile</hi>.
